code: checkOpenEXRFile((const char*) data, size, true, true, true);
note: Fuzzer entry point passes raw input bytes to the EXR file checker, which parses the file header and processes chunks.

code: read magic number and version flags from input
note: The EXR file magic number 20000630 and version field are read from the attacker-controlled input; version must be 2 for the DWA v2 path.

code: parse header attributes including compression type
note: The compression attribute is parsed from the header; setting it to DWAA (8) or DWAB (9) routes decoding to the DWA decompressor.
The DWA decompression entry point receives the raw chunk data from the EXR file, which contains the attacker-controlled DWA compressed block.
The version counter is read from the first 8 bytes of the chunk data (after XDR-to-native conversion). Setting version to 2 triggers the channel rules parsing path.
Since version is 2, the code calls DwaCompressor_readChannelRules with the remaining chunk data, which contains the channel classification rules.
The first 2 bytes of the rules data specify the total rule size. This value is attacker-controlled and must be large enough to contain the malicious classifier data.
The first pass parses classifiers to count them. The attacker-controlled classifier data is passed to Classifier_read, which reads the suffix string.
A 129-byte stack buffer is allocated for the classifier suffix string. The attacker controls the bytes read into this buffer.

The loop reads up to 128 bytes from the input into suffix. If the attacker provides exactly 128 non-null bytes with no null terminator, the loop exits with len=128 after filling all 128 bytes of the buffer.

After the loop, len is incremented from 128 to 129. The check `if (len == 128 + 1)` compares 129 == 129, which would normally catch this case. However, if the loop exits because len reached 128+1=129 (i.e., all 129 bytes were non-null), then len becomes 130 after the increment, bypassing the check.

The check only catches len==129. If the attacker provides exactly 128 non-null bytes followed by a null byte at position 128, the loop breaks at len=128, then len becomes 129, and the check catches it. But if the attacker provides 129 non-null bytes, the loop exits at len=129, then len becomes 130, bypassing the check.

With len=130, the code allocates 130 bytes and calls memcpy(mem, suffix, 130), reading 130 bytes from the 129-byte stack buffer suffix. This reads 1 byte past the end of the stack buffer, causing a stack-buffer-overflow READ.
The memcpy reads 130 bytes from the 129-byte stack buffer. The byte at suffix[129] is out of bounds, triggering the ASAN stack-buffer-overflow READ at this location.
